name: Grail

attributes.attribute: is imagined as the cup of the Last Supper and the vessel of Christ's blood
may descend from Celtic cauldrons of plenty and rebirth
serves as a moral test that only the worthy knight can pass
is healed only when the Grail quest succeeds

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The Holy Grail is a symbolic object pictured as the sacred cup Jesus drank from at the Last Supper. Some tellings describe it as the platter for his bread or the paschal lamb. Others say it caught his blood as he lay dying. Joseph of Arimathea, the merchant who owned the supper house, carried the Grail to Britain. The Christian emblem of transubstantiation then fused with Celtic legends into a complex tale that still moves poets and thinkers. In that tale the Fisher King lies wounded in his body and heals only when the quest is complete. Celtic studies reads the Grail at two levels. The first asks whether older Celtic vessels lie behind it. Loomis and others point to wonder cauldrons that feed or revive: the peir dadeni of Branwen, the chief of Annwn's cauldron in Preiddiau Annwfn, and Diwrnach's vessel in Culhwch ac Olwen. The pearl-rimmed cauldron of the poem will not boil meat for a coward or a liar, a moral test close to the Grail's own. Cauldrons placed in lakes and bogs, as at Llyn Fawr, show that such vessels held ritual weight in Late Bronze and Iron Age deposits. Other scholars read the severed head of the Welsh procession as a trace of the Celtic head cult. The second level is the later Welsh and Irish retelling of French Grail romances.

okr.objective: Set out the Holy Grail as a Christian symbol with Celtic antecedents and a long literary afterlife.
key_results: Record the cup, platter, and blood-vessel forms of the Grail.
Name the Celtic cauldrons proposed as forerunners.
Explain the moral test shared by cauldron and Grail.
Note the Welsh and Irish adaptations of French romances.
